# PeTTa

> MeTTa, Hyperon's AGI language, implemented in SWI-Prolog, with `petta` as its
> Python surface. Atoms are Python values, spaces are queryable stores,
> equations rewrite, and any Python library maps onto those forms. Every line
> below is a signature, an exact return shape, or a contract you cannot guess.
> Names here are checked against the live engine and the real file tree by
> `check.sh`'s `llms` lane, so a rename breaks the build instead of misleading
> you. Counts are dated; treat an undated number as unverified.

## Every source of information in this repository

Prose can drift; the first four rows cannot, because a gate lane regenerates or
re-runs them.

| source | what it is | kept true by |
|---|---|---|

Counts measured 2026-08-19, each one re-checked by the `llms` gate lane on
every run.

## Install and first call

`pip install .` (the runtime is bundled) or point `PETTA_PATH` at a clone.

```python
from petta import MeTTa, S, V, val, expr, parse, cast
m = MeTTa()                      # binds &self, the same space the CLI uses
m.run("(= (f) 1) !(f) !(+ 1 2)") # [[Gnd(1)], [Gnd(3)]]
```

Module-level `petta.run/query/eval/add/remove/parse/fn/trace` act on one lazily
created default engine, for scripts that never need a second space.

## Atoms: built in Python, no engine call

`S.likes` is the symbol `likes`; `S["+"]`, `S["my-name"]` for non-identifiers.
`V.x` is the variable `$x`. `val(obj)` / `Gnd(obj)` wraps a Python value.
Applying a symbol builds an expression: `S.likes(S.Ada, S.Music)` ->
`(likes Ada Music)`. `expr(S.f, 1, 2)` is the same as `S.f(1, 2)`.
`parse("(f $x)")` reads one form without evaluating it.

Four kinds, all immutable with `__slots__` and `__match_args__`, so
`match atom: case Expr(head, args): ...` works: `Sym`, `Var`, `Gnd`, `Expr`.
`Expr.head`, `.args`, `.children`. Free functions in `petta.atoms`:
`alpha_eq`, `unify`, `substitute`, `is_ground`, `map_atoms`, `variables`,
`order_key`, `pretty(atom, width=78)`, `encode`/`decode`, `atom_from_wire`,
`register_object_repr` and `register_object_repr_protocol` (and their
`unregister_` twins) to control how a foreign object prints as an atom.

Operators BUILD terms, they do not compute. `V.age >= 18` is `(>= $age 18)`;
`&` `|` `~` build `and`/`or`/`not`; `+ - * / % **` and `@` build arithmetic
terms. There is no `//`: neither the operator nor an engine builtin exists.
Arithmetic on two grounded values stays ordinary Python. `Expr.__bool__` raises
on comparison and boolean heads, so `if V.x > 1:` is refused rather than
silently truthy. Equality is the one inversion: `a == b` is ordinary Python
comparison answering `True`/`False`, while `a.eq(b)` and `a.ne(b)` build the
MeTTa terms `(== a b)` and `(not (== a b))` for `where=` guards and equations.

The MeTTa `==` is `(-> $a $a Bool)`: it compares two things of ONE type and
refuses two of different KNOWN types by name, so `!(== 1 "S")` raises rather
than answering `False`. An operand nothing declares contradicts nothing, so
`!(== 1 a)` still answers `False`, and expressions are left alone, so
`!(== (collapse ...) ())` is unchanged. `=alpha` is `(-> Atom Atom Bool)` and
takes anything. Python's `a == b` still answers `False` across kinds, because
`__eq__` may not raise.

## Running and querying: exact return shapes

```
m.run(src, using=None, *, timeout=, inferences=, capture=False,
      atomic=False, speculative=False, strict=False)
                       -> list[list[Atom]], one inner list per ! directive
                          (with capture=True: (groups, printed_text))
m.eval(target, *, using=, timeout=, inferences=, capture=False,
       residuals=False)                    -> list[Atom | Undefined]
m.one(target, *, using=, timeout=, inferences=)   -> Any, THE answer as a plain
                          Python value; raises EngineError unless exactly one
m.first(target, *, using=, timeout=, inferences=) -> Any or None
m.query(*patterns, where=, limit=, timeout=, inferences=, into=) -> Rows
m.stream(*patterns, where=, timeout=, inferences=)  -> Cursor, engine-held,
                          lazily iterated, with .columns, .explain() and .close()
m.prepare(*patterns, where=) -> Prepared; .solve(given=...) many times, .columns
m.parse(src) -> Atom
m.load(path, *, timeout=, inferences=) -> list[list[Atom]]
m.save(path, format="metta"|"fast") -> int   (atomic, fsynced)
m.digest() -> str, 64-hex content hash of the space, store-independent
```

`target` may be a string or an already-built atom. `using=` maps BARE SYMBOLS
(not `$vars`) to Python objects, which cross by identity, not by copy or repr:
`m.one("(gated v)", using={"v": tensor})`. It works on `run`, `eval`, `one`,
`first` and their async twins, and is refused together with `residuals=`.

Variables shared across query patterns join: `m.query(S.p(V.x,V.y), S.p(V.y,V.z))`.
`where=` is a term the engine evaluates per match: `where=(V.n >= 60) & (V.n <= 70)`.
`into=` builds each row as that class.

`m.run(..., atomic=True)` makes the whole run one transaction; `speculative=True`
rolls its writes back; `strict=True` raises `StrictError` on a `not-reducible`
directive (opt-in, because an unreduced term is an ordinary MeTTa value).

`Rows` is a list of `Row` with `.columns`. `row.x` and `row["x"]` both work.
`rows.one()` (exactly one), `.first()`, `.column(name)` -> that column's atoms,
`.table()` -> dict of columns decoded to Python values, `.to_dicts()` -> plain
mappings, `.to_df()` / `.to_pl()` -> pandas / polars, `.build(column, cls)`
rebuilds one column as that class and keeps `cls` for type checkers,
`.pipe(fn, *args)` chains, `_repr_html_` renders in notebooks.

`m.assuming(*facts)` is a with-block where those facts exist and then do not.
`m.batch()` collects `add()` calls and crosses once at exit.
`m.limits(timeout=, inferences=)` sets scoped defaults for every call inside.

## Spaces

`m.space(name)` selects; `m.new_space()` creates an unused one and is a context
manager whose exit drops it; `m.copy()` clones contents into a fresh anonymous
space through the bulk door, so equations copy as equations and keep running.
`m.drop()` clears a space and releases its name: a drop clears the whole life,
atoms, equations, subscriptions, import markers and tabling state. Named spaces
compile into their own module, so two spaces can define the same function.
`(context-space)` names the space the running code is in, and
`petta.current_space()` reports it from inside an operation.

`m.add(*atoms)`, `m.remove(atom)`, `m.atoms()`, `m.count()`, `m.clear()`,
`m.space_names()`, `m.space_name`, `m.add_table(head, source)` reads polars /
pandas / mappings / iterables into `(head v1 .. vn)` facts and answers how many.

`petta.spaces` composes spaces without copying: `union(*spaces)` reads a set as
one, `overlay(front, back)` reads both and writes to the front, `readonly(s)`
refuses writes by capability, `mapped(s, shape)` is a shape view from one
declaration, and `diff(a, b)` says HOW two spaces differ where `digest()` only
says THAT they do.

`petta.structures` holds the stores worth having: `AlphaSet` (atoms modulo
variable renaming), `PatternMap` (a MutableMapping keyed by atoms),
`MatchIndex` (many patterns, one atom, which match), `LiveView` (a materialised
view kept current by the space's own writes), `ClosureView` (reachability over a
stored relation), `TabledMap` (a computed cache that stays correct).

`&petta` is the space in which the library describes itself, and it is where
every declaration below is stored. The catalog describes its own kinds there:
`(kind head argspec...)` rows declare each declaration's shape,
`(vocabulary name value...)` rows declare the value sets, and
`(claim vocab value property...)` rows attach per-value facts. One generic
checker validates every `&petta` write against them, a violation is a hard
error naming the atom, the position and the argspec, and a head with no kind
row passes untouched, so third-party declaration kinds are ordinary data
until their author declares a kind row for them.

## Python functions as MeTTa functions

```python
@m.register_op            # alias @m.op
def hypot(a: float, b: float) -> float: ...
```

Options: `name=`, `typed=True`, `raw=False`, `pass_atoms=False`, `arities=`,
`inverse=` (the callable that runs it backwards), `pure=` (declares it free of
effects, which licenses the optimiser). `m.unregister_op(name)` removes every
arity.

The Python name is the MeTTa name, VERBATIM, and nothing is rewritten. Hyphens
are MeTTa's convention and Python cannot spell one, so ask: `name="p-digit"` on
`register_op`, `@m.define(name="p-sum")`, `rename=` on `integrate.module_ops`.
The same holds inside a compiled body, where a called name is resolved exactly
as written, so a hyphenated engine function is reached through an alias
equation the body can spell, `(= (sqrt_math $x) (sqrt-math $x))`.

Annotations become declarations in the engine's idiom: a `TypeVar` is
parametric, a `Union` declares one arrow per member, `Callable[[int],int]` ->
`(-> Number Number)`, `tuple[int,str]` -> elementwise. A generator is
nondeterministic, one answer per yield; returning `None` answers nothing, which
is why an `Optional` return declares the value type.

`@m.define` compiles the Python BODY into MeTTa equations, and `.py` keeps the
plain function; stacked clauses become a first-match dispatcher. It takes
`name=`, and `prolog=` to make a Prolog file the function with the Python kept
as the reference twin.
`@m.type(cls)` declares a class into a space: `(: ...)` atoms, one accessor
equation per field for an expression-image class, and its methods registered as
functions, so the class crosses with its behavior.
`m.fn(name)` calls an engine function from Python (`m.fn("superpose").all(...)`
for every answer; `.compiled` for the clauses).
`m.register_prolog(source=..., path=..., names=...)` registers Prolog
predicates directly, which is the fast path: 7.16 inferences and 0.13us per
call against 25.16 and 2.34us for the same operation through `register_op`.
`m.register_foreign_library(path, entry=, names=)` loads a compiled `.so`.
`m.unregister_prolog(extension)` releases everything one extension registered.

## Types and cast

Types are optional atoms: `(: Ann Person)`, `(: age (-> Person Number))`.
A typed call silently answers empty for a mismatched or `%Undefined%` argument,
so `m.cast(value, type)` is the loud spelling: it returns the value or raises
`CastError` naming the types the value does admit. `Atom`, `%Undefined%` and `_`
are unchecked. A float or signed-i64 integer has type `Number`; a wider integer
has type `BigInt`. A `BigInt` satisfies a declared `Number` parameter, while a
`Number` does not satisfy `BigInt`. Arithmetic stays exact and result typing
follows the result width. `bool` spells `Bool` before `int` is classified by
that boundary. The target is positional-only, and a concrete Python class
target is also the static return type of `cast`, `convert.build` and
`Rows.build`.
`m.arities(name)`, `m.is_function(name)` (visible from here),
`m.is_function_here(name)` (has clauses HERE), `m.builtins()`.

## Declarations: how a space behaves, written as atoms

Each `m.declare_*` writes one atom into `&petta` and returns it; removing that
atom withdraws the declaration. Coherence is checked eagerly in the same
transaction as the write, so a new entry that could disagree with an existing
one fails there, naming both, rather than on the first query in their overlap.

```
declare_handles(name, pattern, "Exact"|"Partial"|"Sound"|"Refuse", det=)
        how faithfully a space answers one query shape. Exact licenses pushing
        the caller's bound down to the provider; Partial and Sound stay
        candidates the engine re-unifies; Refuse makes the query a loud error
        instead of a silent partial answer. (in $x) at a position matches only
        queries arriving with it bound, so a scan-only source is three words.
declare_emits(name, "depth"|"fair"|"best-first")     answer order
declare_merge(pattern, "depth"|"fair"|"best-first")  how answers merge
declare_source(name, "linear"|"repeated"|"peek")     consumption discipline
declare_writes(name, "transactional"|"atomic-single"|"best-effort")
declare_context(name, "closed-world"|"open-world")   what absence means
declare_on_error(name, pattern, "keep"|"empty"|"abort")
declare_annotations(name, "bool"|"bag"|"set"|"ranked"|"prob"|"prov")
        the semiring answer annotations live in: this is how a space carries
        scores, probabilities or provenance instead of plain truth
declare_admits(name, type_name)     only TYPE-carrying atoms enter
declare_capacity(name, limit)       an add beyond LIMIT is refused loudly
declare_reaction(name, pattern, operation)   stored as an (on ...) atom
```

## Observability

```
m.trace(src, max_events=1_000_000) -> list[TraceEvent(depth, kind, term, answer)]
        kinds "call" and "exit"; a reduction that fails leaves a call with no exit
m.derivation(target, depth=None, *, timeout=, inferences=) -> list[Derivation]
        proof trees in MeTTa terms: .rules, .facts, .complete, .truncations
m.why(pattern) -> str            one empty match explained in words
rows.why()                       pattern miss, failed join, or rejecting guard
m.lint() -> list[lint.Finding]   the silently-wrong class, from stored structure
petta.lint.lint_file(path, m=None)   the same findings anchored to file:line
m.eval_status(target) / m.run_status(src)  each answer paired with the path that
        produced it: "value" (equation, builtin or special form applied),
        "not-reducible" (no rule applied, the answer is the term itself),
        "empty" (branch pruned, answer None). A pruned branch and an unevaluated
        term are different things the answers alone cannot tell apart.
m.stats()      with-block yielding .inferences (deterministic, gate on this),
               .cputime, .walltime, .gc_count, .gc_freed, .gc_time, .table_bytes
m.profile(src) -> (groups, EngineProfile), per predicate
m.profile_extension(src, extension=, names=)  only YOUR functions
m.disassemble(name) -> str    the Prolog clauses a function compiled to
m.prolog()                    the engine's own interactive toplevel
petta.backend_info() -> versions of petta, janus, swi_prolog, python, petta_path
```

Errors: `PettaError` is the base, then `EngineError`, `MettaSyntaxError`,
`CastError`, `CompileError`, `StrictError`, `SourceNotFound`,
`MettaResultError`, `TransportFailure`, and `ResourceLimitError` with
`TimeLimitError` and `InferenceLimitError` under it, plus `Interrupted`.
`MettaOperationError(EngineError)` is a builtin refusing a value, with the parts
as data: `.operation` is what the source wrote (`+`, `min-atom`), `.kind` the
formal's functor, `.expected` and `.culprit` the type and offending value.
`DECLINE` / `Decline` is how a provider says "not mine" rather than failing.
Type checkers get `SpaceName`, `MettaName` and the closed `SaveFormat` set,
all constructible straight from `petta`.

## Concurrency, transactions, bounds

Engine calls belong to the thread that made the engine. `m.pool(workers)` gives
each worker its OWN attached engine, which is what makes the calls genuinely
concurrent (measured 2026-08-15: 1.94x, 3.90x and 7.26x at 2, 4 and 8 workers).
`m.parallel(*targets)` and its language-side name `m.hyperpose(*targets)`
evaluate targets at once. `petta.aio.AsyncMeTTa` runs engine calls on one worker
thread behind `async`; `petta.engine_thread()` and `petta.current_space()`
report the crossing.

In MeTTa, `(transaction EXPR)` and `(atomically EXPR)` run one atomic block.
Both answer EVERY answer their body has and commit or roll back the whole
answer set; `transaction` compiles its body into the call site, `atomically`
takes the body as an unreduced atom and evaluates it, so only `atomically`
can run a body the program computed.

`m.transaction(callable)` and the `@m.transactional` decorator run a callable in
one engine transaction. Control signals cannot be eaten by the evaluation they
stop, not even by a program's own `(catch ...)`: a bound, a Ctrl-C and an
`interrupt()` all reach a running goal, the same reasoning that puts
`KeyboardInterrupt` outside `Exception`.

## Integrating any library

`petta.convert`: `project(obj) -> Projected` whose `.atom` is the constructor
expression, `build(atom)` -> object (returning the atom unchanged when it
cannot), `register_type`, `unregister_type`, `declarations`, `auto_image`.
Dataclasses, enums, pydantic models and annotated classes all cross; enums
project to symbols. `@petta.record` marks a class for the round trip.

`petta.integrate`: `module_ops(m, module, names=, prefix=, rename=, raw=True,
typed=False)` registers a whole module's callables, `facts(m, atoms)` bulk-writes,
`wrap_object(m, name, obj, methods)`, `reflect(m, name, obj)`,
`install_reflection_ops(m)`, `integrate(m, target)`, `Integration`,
`SpaceProvider`, and `discover(m)` over entry points. Installation is idempotent
for a live space, and dropping a space releases its installation record.
Entry-point groups: `petta.integrations`, `petta.spaces`, `petta.libraries`.

`petta.arrays`: one operation vocabulary over any DLPack library.
`install(m, default=xp)` makes numpy, torch or JAX first-class with the same
words; `namespace_of`, `is_array`, `data_of`, `ARRAY_OPS`, and `EmbeddingStore`
with an exact faiss backend.

`petta.tables`: `declare(...)` writes one ctx-scoped bridge declaration into
`&petta` and `TableBridge` derives every provider operation from it, so a
DB-API connection (the `Executes` slice) answers MeTTa matches.
`petta.persistent.PersistentFactSpace` is journalled and crash-recovering.
`petta.das` is SingularityNET's Distributed Atomspace as a space.

## Foreign spaces and the backend seam

A space can be backed by anything, and the seam is universal rather than
per-backend. From Python, implement `Matcher` / `Enumerable` / `Adder` /
`BulkAdder` / `Remover` / `Clearer` / `Planner` / `Transactional` / `CustomMatch`
and call `petta.foreign.register_provider(runtime, name, provider)` with a name
starting with `&`; or subclass `SpaceProvider` and answer `can_run` per call.
Capabilities are declared, not guessed: `match`, `enumerate`, `add`, `add-many`,
`remove`, `clear`, `subscribe`, `plan`, `rules`, and an unsupported operation
refuses loudly rather than degrading. Conjunctive queries route per conjunct, so
a foreign space joins with a native one; on such a conjunction `rows.why()`
prints which conjunct went where and whether its class was exact.

From Prolog, `src/ext_points.pl` declares every seam WITH ITS KIND: an EVENT runs
for effect and every handler runs; an OWNERSHIP seam is claimed by the first
handler that succeeds and declined by failing; a DECLARATION is a fact table read
as data; a SERVICE runs the other way, a predicate the ENGINE defines that an
extension may CALL. The service list is the whole permitted inward surface
(`swrite/2`, `sread/2`, `metta_symbol_writable/1`, `metta_unwritable_symbol/2`,
`throw_metta_type_error/3`, `rethrow_metta_operation_error/2`,
`current_metta_module/1`, `space_module/2`, `metta_module_space/2`,
`petta_shape_route/5`, the routed view of any shape-routed declaration
kind), and it exists so a backend never reaches into
`src/parser.pl`, the same reason SQLite hands extensions an
`sqlite3_api_routines` table instead of letting them link against internals.

`backends/*.pl` is globbed at boot and each file decides for itself whether its
own artefact is present, so there is no backend "mode" to select and the engine
names no backend. A MORK-backed store is one such backend, supplying `&mork` and
`&mork:name`; it is present only when its shared library was built.

## Apps, from source

`petta.manifest.boot(manifest, m=None, connections=, host=, token=, authorize=,
ssl_context=)` assembles an app from `(boot ...)` forms, each sugar for exactly
one existing call, performed in source order:

```
(boot (load "rules.metta"))                m.load, manifest-relative
(boot (attach &crm "http://crm:8700"))     petta.remote.attach
(boot (bridge &db (edge $a $b) (row ...))) petta.tables declare + bridge
(boot (serve (&self &crm) 8700))           petta.remote.serve
```

The vocabulary is closed and validated whole before anything runs; bridged names
must appear in `connections` and every connection must be claimed. Each
performed form is stored as its own atom, so the running app answers
`(match &self (boot $what) $what)` with its own topology. A manifest that fails
mid-way keeps its performed prefix's writes, closes any servers it started, and
names the failing form.

`python -m petta` has six subcommands: `run` (files, printing each `!` answer
group), `repl` (paren-balance aware, readline), `serve`, `boot`, `lint` (nonzero
exit on findings), `doc` (a name's `(@doc ...)`).

`petta.remote`: `serve(m, spaces=, token=, authorize=, ssl_context=)`,
`connect(url, token=, headers=)`, `attach`. Credentials require https, tokens
compare in constant time, and only http/https schemes are accepted.

`petta.subscribe`: `m.subscribe(pattern, callback, on="add", queue_max=10000)`
is a standing query delivered INSIDE the write that matched it; without a
callback, events queue until `drain()`, and a full queue raises rather than
discarding the oldest. A callback that raises reaches the writer as
`SubscriberError`, which carries `.subscription` and says the write was
applied, so it is not a failed write and retrying it duplicates.
`bridge(...)` connects two spaces. `Subscription` is a context manager and
also a blocking event stream. A `RemoteSpace` refuses `subscribe`: there is
no event channel on the wire.

The wire has both doors the in-process seam has. `RemoteSpace.match` is
eager, one request carrying the whole answer set, and `RemoteSpace.stream`
is the protocol's ask/next/stop lifecycle, a chunk per request, so taking
two answers of a large enumeration costs the serving engine two answers.
`petta.remote.attach(m, name, url, batch=1)` puts an attached space's
matching on the lazy door. `petta.remote.Gateway` is the same protocol with
no transport under it, for mounting on another HTTP framework.
`website/live/remote-protocol.md` is the contract every binding inherits and
`petta.testing.GatewayComplianceSuite` certifies it.

`petta.testing` ships what the suite fuzzes itself with: hypothesis strategies
(`atoms`, `expressions`, `patterns`, `names`, `numbers`, `texts`, `symbols`,
`variables`, `grounded`, `ground_atoms`, `numpy_scalars`), the compliance suites
(`SpaceComplianceSuite`, `GatewayComplianceSuite`, `check_space_provider`,
`check_twin`, `check_replay`, `check_minted_handles`), and the deterministic
benchmark gates (`benchmark_case`, `benchmark_counter_slope`,
`measure_instructions`, `BenchmarkBaseline`, `count_atoms`), also exported from
`petta.benchmarking`. `petta.pytest_plugin` gives the `metta` and
`scratch_space` fixtures; `petta.ipython` gives `%%metta` in a notebook.

Eleven submodules load on first access rather than during `import petta`:
`aio`, `arrays`, `das`, `manifest`, `parallel`, `persistent`, `remote`, `spaces`,
`structures`, `tables`, `testing`, and `boot` resolves the same way.

Importing petta therefore never pulls in the HTTP and table machinery boot
composes over. dir(petta) still lists each one, and subscribe is eager, being
part of the write path.

## The MeTTa language surface

Special forms are compiled by the translator rather than defined by equations,
and most answer false to "is this a function", so "no equations" does not mean
"nothing can prove it":

```
if case let let* collapse superpose quote sealed unify match
once forall foldall not-provable prog1 progn nop cut super
chain eval evalc noeval reduce filter-atom foldl-atom map-atom
add-atom add-atoms add-reduct add-reducts remove-atom get-metatype
catch timeout inferences elapsed take top transaction with-pragma!
with_mutex hyperpose call explain annotation test test-no-answer
translatePredicate |->
```

Eight more are written in MeTTa, as prelude equations saying what the call
expands to: `and-then`, `or-else`, `trace!`, `unique`, `alpha-unique`,
`union`, `intersection`, `subtraction`.

Each of those is an ordinary equation plus one registration, and KERNEL.md is
the ledger of which head is which, what it answers to in the minimal
instruction set the arbiter presents, and for a derived form still fused into
the compiler, the measurement that keeps it there.

221 builtins are registered (`m.builtins()` lists them live), among them the
py-* bridge (`py-atom`, `py-call`, `py-dot`, `py-iter`, `py-len`, `py-list`,
`py-dict`, `py-tuple`, `py-str`, `py-repr`, `py-format`, `py-slice`, `py-range`,
`py-at`, `py-in`, `py-eq`, `py-truthy`, `py-round`, `py-str-join`), the atom
algebra (`car-atom`, `cdr-atom`, `cons-atom`, `decons-atom`, `index-atom`,
`size-atom`, `sort-atom`, `union-atom`, `intersection-atom`, `subtraction-atom`,
`unique-atom`, `max-atom`, `min-atom`), the assert family
(`assertEqual`, `assertAlphaEqual`, `assertEqualToResult`, `assertIncludes`) that the
example corpus is written in, `get-type`, `get-doc`, `help!`, `import!`, `pragma!`, `bind!`,
`new-space`, `get-state` / `change-state!`, `pretty-atom`, `random-int` /
`random-float`, `format-time`, and the CLP(FD) relations (`#+`, `#-`, `#*`,
`#//`, `#div`, `#mod`, `#<`, `#=<`, `#>`, `#>=`, `#=`, `#\=`, `#min`, `#max`),
which RELATE rather than compute, so giving any two of three solves the third.

Hand a builtin an unbound variable where it needs a value and it refuses by
name: `!(car-atom $u)` is `car-atom: a value expected in argument 1, found an
unbound variable`. The guarded positions are derived from the type surface
(`guarded_input_position/3`, 83 of them), so a position declared `Expression`,
`Number`, `BigInt`, `String`, `Symbol` or `Bool` is an input to read. What stays
relational is named in the engine: `index-atom`'s index, the boolean
operations' truth table, `cons`'s open tail, `union-atom` and `member`, which
are `append/3` and `member/2` under MeTTa names, the `#` family throughout,
and every name lent to MeTTa from SWI (`msort`, `append`, `sort`, `maplist`,
`length`), which under that name IS the Prolog predicate.

32 libraries load with `!(import! &self (library lib_x))`: `lib_builtin_types`,
`lib_combinatorics`, `lib_conformance`, `lib_constraints`, `lib_crypto`,
`lib_datastructures`, `lib_datetime`, `lib_derived`, `lib_doc`, `lib_file`,
`lib_he`,
`lib_import`, `lib_json`, `lib_llm`, `lib_measure`, `lib_memo`, `lib_mm2`,
`lib_nars`, `lib_patrick`, `lib_pln`, `lib_redis`, `lib_reflect`, `lib_regex`,
`lib_roman`, `lib_soft`, `lib_spaces`, `lib_string`, `lib_tabling`, `lib_thread`,
`lib_torch`, `lib_vector`, `lib_zar`. Scored answers and fuzzy or regex matching
are `lib_measure` and `lib_regex` riding the general seam, not Python modules:
there is no `petta.measure` and no `petta.matching`.

## Contracts that cost real debugging

`match` evaluates its space and its body, never its pattern: patterns are
structural, so compute first and match after with `let`.
MeTTa equations ACCUMULATE. Redefining a function ADDS an alternative rather
than replacing the old one, so a second `(= (f x) ...)` gives `f` two answers.
Equations are alternatives, not sequential clauses; a literal-headed default
needs a guard or it fires too.
A typed call rejects a bad argument by answering empty, not by raising: use `cast`.
An unreduced call is a non-empty answer, so test truth with `any(a == True)`,
never "the result was non-empty".
Python `None` from an operation answers nothing.
`(empty)` yields no answer at all, which is how a branch prunes itself.
`collapse` is a special form because ordinary arguments evaluate eagerly: a
helper "around" `collapse` collapses an already-chosen answer, so inline it.
`forall` stops its generator when the check fails (it compiles to Prolog's
`\+ (Gen, \+ Test)`), so a bounded take over an infinite producer is writable
and terminates where `collapse` cannot run at all.
`py-iter` is lazy and yields one answer at a time; a Python generator is not
drained. `py-atom` takes a metatype argument, `Grounded` for the live reference
and `Expression` for a snapshot.
Strings carry hyperon's five escapes (quote, backslash, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`).
Symbols containing whitespace, parentheses or quotes are refused at save and
digest rather than written unreadably.

## Measuring

Wall clock under ~100ms is bimodal on a loaded box and has produced false
results here twice. `m.stats().inferences` is deterministic (five runs of one
workload gave 1,000,601 every time, 0.0000% spread, while wall clock swung
6.86%), so gate on inferences and let wall clock advise. For pure-Python paths
where the engine does nothing, use `perf stat -e instructions:u`. Instruction
counts move with code LAYOUT, so perturb with inert clauses before believing a
regression. Check `/proc/loadavg` before trusting any timing.

## Downstream packages built on this surface

`pettorch` connects PyTorch through `petta.arrays` and `petta.integrate` and
adds autograd operations, module wrappers, training helpers and neural
predicates; `website/guide/pettorch.md` is its page here.
`petta-fabric-pc` projects a FabricPC predictive-coding network into a space, so
settling, attention and comparison are MeTTa rather than Python.
Neither is a special case in the engine: both are ordinary users of
`register_op`, `arrays.install`, `integrate.facts` and the provider seam.
